power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

The study was approved by the University of Virginia Institutional Review Board for Social and Behavioral Sciences (protocol #6471; approved April 17, 2024), and all participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two counterbalanced sequences.
Participants provided demographic data and were fitted with a mobile EEG headset before beginning the two pod exposures (Fig. 2).
A researcher followed responses using a correct-answer sheet; participants were not systematically corrected or restarted after errors.
Of 72 possible pod recordings, 68 recordings from 35 participants were available and successfully preprocessed; 33 participants contributed recordings in both pods (Table A.4).
Participants completed a brief serial-subtraction task followed by a pre-immersion questionnaire before a 10-min seated immersion in the assigned pod.
After immersion, participants completed a post-immersion questionnaire.

text.text: Exposure to natural environments has been associated with benefits for health and wellbeing, and natural materials offer one avenue for introducing nature-associated elements into interiors.
However, relatively little in situ research has examined subjective and neural responses to full-scale interiors with contrasting material characteristics.

In this within-subject crossover study, 36 students completed 10-min immersions in wood-clad and white drywall prototype pods following a mental arithmetic task while self-report data and mobile electroencephalography (EEG) were collected.
Adjusted models indicated greater momentary nature connectedness and perceived restorative qualities in the wood-clad pod, as well as higher hedonic tone and energetic arousal and lower stress.
The primary frontal EEG measures did not differ significantly between pods after correction for multiple comparisons.

Together, these findings show that contrasting full-scale interiors elicited distinct immediate subjective responses without corresponding robust differences in selected frontal EEG measures, highlighting the value of multimodal in situ approaches for studying architectural experience.

text.text: Restorative-environment theories propose that certain environmental characteristics may support recovery from cognitive and affective demands.

Stress Reduction Theory emphasizes affective and physiological recovery from stress, whereas Attention Restoration Theory emphasizes recovery of directed attention through qualities including separation from routine demands (being away), effortless attentional engagement (fascination), perceived coherence and scope (extent), and fit between the environment and an individual's purposes (compatibility) (Kaplan and Kaplan, 1989; Ulrich et al., 1991).

text.text: Much of the evidence for restorative environments concerns outdoor nature or visual exposure to natural scenes.
While nature exposure has been associated with mental, cognitive, and physical health benefits (Jimenez et al., 2021), much of daily life is spent indoors.

text.text: Biophilic design seeks to incorporate nature and nature-associated features into built environments through strategies such as natural materials, vegetation, views, and natural forms (Browning et al., 2014).

text.text: Material choices are directly actionable in architectural practice and may offer a relatively accessible means of influencing occupants' experiences across diverse building settings.
Wood has received particular attention in this context.

Prior research suggests that wooden interior materials can influence environmental appraisal, including perceived comfort and preference, as well as affective responses and autonomic physiology (Alapieti et al., 2020; Nyrud and Bringslimark, 2010).

text.text: A small but growing body of research has examined responses during direct occupancy of full-scale wooden and non-wooden interiors, reporting differences in affective and perceptual responses and, in some studies, autonomic physiology, although findings have varied across outcomes (Demattè et al., 2018; Kumpulainen et al., 2024; Ojala et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2016).

text.text: Responses may also depend on the amount, visual characteristics, and context of wood exposure; for example, a full-scale room study found that moderate wood coverage tended to receive higher comfort ratings than either no wood or extensive wood coverage (Tsunetsugu et al., 2007).

text.text: Despite this emerging literature on full-scale experiments, studies conducted in real-world architectural settings remain comparatively limited, and neural responses to contrasting interior environments have received little attention (Norwood et al., 2019; Senkler et al., 2025).

text.text: It therefore remains unclear whether subjective differences during occupancy are accompanied by measurable differences in neural activity.
Mobile EEG provides a means of examining this question during direct occupancy while retaining the multisensory and spatial qualities of architectural experience.
At the same time, studying full-scale environments in situ involves a tradeoff between ecological validity and experimental control because individual design features are more difficult to isolate.

Environmental neuroscience research has examined neural responses to natural and built environments, including virtual representations of these settings, using methods such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) (Li et al., 2021; Norwood et al., 2019).

text.text: Whereas fMRI scanner-based and virtual approaches do not fully reproduce occupancy of a real architectural environment, mobile EEG allows neural activity to be measured during more naturalistic environmental exposure.

While many studies still rely on laboratory-based representations of real-world settings, an increasing number use mobile EEG to examine neural responses during real-world environmental exposure (Aspinall et al., 2015; Mavros et al., 2022; Neale et al., 2020).

text.text: Although mobile EEG enables neural activity to be examined during direct environmental exposure, commonly used frequency-domain measures do not map uniquely onto psychological constructs such as relaxation or stress recovery, and their interpretation is context dependent (Senkler et al., 2025; Vanhollebeke et al., 2022).

text.text: The present study therefore treated EEG outcomes as complementary measures of neural activity rather than direct biomarkers of psychological restoration.

Frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) was selected as a candidate measure of affective response based on its established use in affective neuroscience and associations with approach-withdrawal processes (Reznik and Allen, 2018).

text.text: The present study examined subjective and neural responses during occupancy of two fullscale prototype pods: a wood-clad pod and a white drywall pod.

Using self-report measures and mobile EEG within a semi-controlled architectural setting, we examined differences in mood, connectedness to nature, perceived restorativeness, and frontal EEG frequencydomain measures and derived indices.
The study had two complementary aims.
First, we examined whether subjective responses differed between the wood-clad and drywall pods.
Second, we examined whether frontal EEG measures differed between pods during occupancy.
We tested the following hypotheses: H1: Self-reported mood would differ between pods, with higher hedonic tone, lower stress, and lower energetic arousal following occupancy of the wood-clad pod.
H2: Momentary connectedness to nature would differ between pods, with higher connectedness following occupancy of the wood-clad pod.
H3: Perceived restorative qualities would differ between pods, with higher ratings for the woodclad pod.
H4: Primary frontal EEG measures would differ between pods during immersion.

text.text: Thirty-six students (28 female; age 18-40 years, M = 22.9, SD = 4.23) were recruited from a large public university in the mid-Atlantic United States through flyers, word of mouth, and a participant pool.
Participant-pool students received course credit; other participants received $20.
Current student enrollment was the sole inclusion criterion.
Sample size was determined pragmatically by access to the prototype pods and participant availability.
We aimed to recruit at least 30 participants.
A within-subject crossover design was used so that each participant experienced both pods.
Data were collected in April-May 2024.

The study was approved by the University of Virginia Institutional Review Board for Social and Behavioral Sciences (protocol #6471; approved April 17, 2024), and all participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.

Participants experienced two prototype pods during a single study visit: a wood-clad pod and a white drywall-paneled pod located next to one another within an open-plan area of an academic building (Fig. 1).

text.text: The pods shared the same overall layout, dimensions, orientation, open entryway, tapered ceiling with a small open skylight, and integrated seating location.

Materiality was the primary intended contrast and extended to the integrated seating: the drywall pod incorporated a drywall-finished bench, whereas the wood-clad pod incorporated a bench composed of transverse-cut logs.
Minor differences in daylight exposure, scent, and other perceptual characteristics also remained.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two counterbalanced sequences.
Exposures were separated by a 20-min standardized break.
Exposure period and randomized sequence were included as adjustment terms in the primary statistical models; sequence was not interpreted as a formal test of carryover.
Participants provided demographic data and were fitted with a mobile EEG headset before beginning the two pod exposures (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Participants provided demographic data and were fitted with a mobile EEG headset before beginning the two pod exposures (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Each pod exposure began with a 2.5-min mental arithmetic task in which participants repeatedly subtracted 7 from 700 as quickly and accurately as possible while responding aloud.
A researcher followed responses using a correct-answer sheet; participants were not systematically corrected or restarted after errors.

The task was intended to induce a mild stress response prior to pod immersion; serial subtraction has been used as the mental-arithmetic component of laboratory stress paradigms (Kirschbaum et al., 1993).
text.formatted: The task was intended to induce a mild stress response prior to pod immersion; serial subtraction has been used as the mental-arithmetic component of laboratory stress paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kirschbaum et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Participants then completed a pre-immersion survey, entered the assigned pod, and remained seated for 10 min while EEG was recorded continuously.
They were instructed to observe the environment while avoiding electronic device use, eating, drinking, and excessive movement.
A post-immersion survey was completed inside the pod.
During the 20-min break, all participants watched the same cartoon and the EEG headset was removed, re-wetted, and refitted before the second pod exposure.

Mood was assessed before and after each immersion using a 12-item abbreviated version of the University of Wales Institute of Science and Technology Mood Adjective Checklist (UWIST-MACL; Matthews et al., 1990).

text.text: Three four-item subscales assessed energetic arousal, stress, and hedonic tone, with higher scores indicating greater energetic arousal, stress, and positive hedonic tone, respectively.

Momentary connectedness to nature was assessed before and after immersion using the single-item Inclusion of Nature in Self Scale (INS; Schultz, 2001), a validated pictorial measure depicting progressively greater overlap between circles representing "Self" and "Nature."

text.text: Higher scores indicate greater perceived connectedness to nature.

Perceived restorative qualities were assessed after each immersion using a 15-item version of the Perceived Restorativeness Scale based on Hartig et al. (1997), comprising Being Away (2 items), Fascination (4), Extent (4), and Compatibility (5).

Time-frequency decomposition used a continuous analytic Morlet wavelet applied before extraction of experimental periods.
Power was calculated as log10-transformed squared wavelet magnitude.
The 2.5-min serial-subtraction period and 10-min immersion period were extracted; immersion was additionally divided into four successive 2.5-min intervals for secondary time-course analyses.
Frequency bands were defined as theta (4-7 Hz), alpha (8-12 Hz), and beta (13-30 Hz), with beta additionally subdivided exploratorily into low beta (13-19 Hz) and high beta (20-30 Hz).
Primary EEG outcomes were F4-F3 frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA), frontal alpha power, and frontal beta power.
Exploratory outcomes included F8-F7 and Fp2-Fp1 FAA, frontal midline theta at Fz, low beta, high beta, and log theta-beta ratio.
Frontal power measures were averaged across F3, Fz, and F4 where applicable.

This in situ crossover study compared subjective and mobile EEG responses between woodclad and drywall prototype pod interiors.

The clearest pod differences emerged in subjective responses: adjusted models indicated greater momentary connectedness to nature and perceived restorative qualities in the wood-clad pod, along with differences in mood.
By contrast, the primary EEG measures did not differ robustly between pods.
The most consistent self-report differences concerned momentary nature connectedness and perceived restorative qualities, supporting H2 and largely supporting H3.
Participants reported greater post-immersion nature connectedness in the wood-clad pod and rated it higher on Being Away, Fascination, and Compatibility; Extent did not differ.
These findings indicate that participants subjectively experienced the two pod interiors differently.
The absence of an Extent difference is also consistent with the physical similarity of the two pods.
Extent specifically concerns perceived coherence and scope, and the pods shared the same general design and dimensions.
Thus, the material and perceptual contrast between the interiors may have been more salient for Being Away, Fascination, and Compatibility than for Extent.

The present findings are broadly consistent with prior full-scale occupancy studies reporting differences in affective and environmental appraisal between wooden and non-wooden interiors (Demattè et al., 2018; Kumpulainen et al., 2024; Ojala et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The present findings are broadly consistent with prior full-scale occupancy studies reporting differences in affective and environmental appraisal between wooden and non-wooden interiors <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Demattè et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kumpulainen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Ojala et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Zhang et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The greater momentary nature connectedness and perceived restorative qualities observed here extend this literature to appraisals of nature connection and restorative environmental qualities.

The perceived-restorativeness findings are also broadly consistent with Attention Restoration Theory, particularly its emphasis on being away, fascination, extent, and compatibility as qualities of restorative settings, although these ratings reflect perceived restorative qualities rather than direct evidence of cognitive restoration (Kaplan and Kaplan, 1989).
text.formatted: The perceived-restorativeness findings are also broadly consistent with Attention Restoration Theory, particularly its emphasis on being away, fascination, extent, and compatibility as qualities of restorative settings, although these ratings reflect perceived restorative qualities rather than direct evidence of cognitive restoration <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Kaplan and Kaplan, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: H1 received partial support.
Adjusted models indicated higher hedonic tone and lower stress in the wood-clad pod, consistent with the predicted directions, but energetic arousal was also higher, contrary to the hypothesis.
In the context of higher hedonic tone, elevated energetic arousal may reflect positive activation or engagement rather than a uniformly relaxed state.
Taken together, the self-report findings indicate that the two occupied pods elicited distinguishable short-term subjective experiences.

Because materiality was the primary intended contrast but other perceptual differences remained, these findings are best interpreted in relation to the contrasting material character of the two pods rather than as effects of wood cladding in isolation.
The primary EEG findings did not support H4.
F4-F3 FAA, frontal alpha power, and frontal beta power did not differ significantly between the wood-clad and drywall pods after FDR correction.
Exploratory TBR showed nominal evidence of a pod effect in both the 10-min immersion and time-course analyses, but neither effect survived correction within the exploratory EEG family.
These TBR findings should therefore be considered hypothesisgenerating rather than evidence of a robust pod-related neural effect.
Several EEG measures also differed between the pre-immersion serial-subtraction task and subsequent immersion (Table A.5).
text.formatted: Several EEG measures also differed between the pre-immersion serial-subtraction task and subsequent immersion <ref type="bibr">(Table A.5</ref>).

text.text: These task-to-immersion differences should not be interpreted as evidence of physiological stress recovery.
The intended stress induction was not independently validated, and participants spoke during serial subtraction but not during immersion.

The observed differences may therefore reflect changes in cognitive demand, attentional state, speech-related muscle activity, or other task-related electrophysiological processes, in addition to any change in stress.
The divergence between subjective and EEG findings is itself informative.
Clear differences in perceived restorative qualities and nature connectedness were not accompanied by robust differences in the primary EEG measures.
This suggests that subjective appraisal and the selected EEG measures may capture different components of environmental experience or differ in sensitivity to the contrast examined here.
One possible explanation is the magnitude of the environmental contrast.
Previous mobile EEG studies have often examined more pronounced environmental contrasts, such as natural versus urban settings (Aspinall et al., 2015; Mavros et al., 2022; Neale et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Previous mobile EEG studies have often examined more pronounced environmental contrasts, such as natural versus urban settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aspinall et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Mavros et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Neale et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The lack of robust EEG differences in the present study may therefore reflect the magnitude of the environmental contrast, limited metric-specific sample sizes, the particular neural measures examined, or some combination of these factors.

From an architectural perspective, the findings suggest that differences between interiors can be reflected in occupants' subjective experience even when corresponding differences are not evident in selected neural measures.
This distinction is important for environmental neuroscience: the absence of a detectable EEG difference should not be taken to imply that occupants experienced the environments similarly.
Several limitations constrain interpretation.
First, the relatively homogeneous sample limits generalizability, and metric-specific missing EEG data reduced the analytic sample sizes and statistical power for neural outcomes.
Larger and more diverse samples will be needed to evaluate smaller neurophysiological effects.
Second, although materiality was the primary intended contrast between the wood-clad and drywall prototypes, the pods were not matched on all perceptual and environmental characteristics.
For example, minor differences in daylight exposure remained.

Accordingly, the observed differences should be interpreted primarily in relation to the contrasting material character of the two pods, while recognizing that other environmental differences may also have contributed.
Future studies should isolate individual design features where feasible or quantify characteristics such as illuminance, acoustics, temperature, and other relevant environmental conditions.
Third, participants could not be blinded to the visibly different pods, and expectancy, environmental preference, perceived naturalness, novelty, and beliefs about study purpose were not measured.
These factors may therefore have contributed to the observed self-report differences.

Finally, the study did not include a neutral resting EEG baseline or an independent manipulation check specifically establishing that the serial-subtraction task increased stress, limiting interpretation of task-to-immersion EEG differences.
The EEG headset was removed and refitted between pod exposures, introducing potential session-specific variation despite quality control and adjustment for task-period EEG.
In addition, the 10-min immersion captured only an acute response.

Future studies incorporating validated manipulation checks, resting baselines, longer or repeated exposures, and more stable physiological measurement could better determine how architectural context influences both immediate and sustained responses.

Wood-clad and drywall prototype pod interiors elicited distinguishable subjective responses during short-term occupancy, particularly in perceived restorative qualities and momentary connectedness to nature, while corresponding differences were not detected in the primary EEG measures.

The findings underscore the potential for material and environmental characteristics of interiors to shape occupants' immediate experience and demonstrate the value of evaluating architectural environments through complementary subjective and neurophysiological measures.
Future research combining ecologically valid occupancy with tighter environmental control will be important for identifying the specific design features contributing to these responses.

text.text: Continuous recordings were band-pass filtered from 1 to 40 Hz and downsampled to 500 Hz.
No separate line-noise correction was applied; analyses were restricted to frequencies below 40 Hz.
Poor-quality channels were identified using clean_rawdata with a flatline criterion of 5 s and a channel-correlation criterion of .75.
Timewindow rejection was disabled to preserve the continuous recordings and event timing.
Artifact subspace reconstruction was applied conservatively using a burst criterion of 40; burstcontaminated data were reconstructed rather than temporally removed (Chang et al., 2020).

text.text: Channels identified as poor quality were removed before independent component analysis (ICA); A2 was also removed before ICA in all analyzed recordings.
Retained scalp channels were average-referenced.
ICA dimensionality was adjusted to the effective rank of the retained data following channel removal and re-referencing, and the data were then decomposed using extended Infomax ICA (runica).
Independent components were classified using ICLabel (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019) and fitted with equivalent dipoles using DIPFIT for quality-control characterization.
text.formatted: Independent components were classified using ICLabel <ref type="bibr">(Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)</ref> and fitted with equivalent dipoles using DIPFIT for quality-control characterization.

text.text: To reduce the risk of over-cleaning in the low-density mobile EEG data, automated IC rejection was limited to high-confidence artifact components, defined as components classified by ICLabel as muscle, eye, heart, line noise, or channel noise with probability ≥ .85.
Components not meeting these criteria were retained.
Low brainclassification probability and dipole residual variance were recorded for quality control but were not used as standalone criteria for automatic component rejection.
Following artifact-component removal, previously removed channels were interpolated using spherical interpolation to restore the original scalp montage, and the data were averagereferenced again.

Interpolation was used to preserve montage consistency rather than to substitute for measured activity: when an electrode required for a particular EEG metric had been removed and subsequently interpolated, that metric was treated as missing for that participant-session.
Session-level quality-control records included channels removed, components rejected, recording duration, event preservation, and metric-specific electrode validity.

For time-frequency analysis, a continuous wavelet transform using the analytic Morlet wavelet (amor) was applied to the full continuous preprocessed recording before extraction of the experimental periods.
Performing the transform before window extraction reduced waveletedge effects at the boundaries between the serial-subtraction and immersion periods.
Power was calculated as the squared magnitude of the wavelet coefficients and log10-transformed.
The 2.5-min serial-subtraction period and 10-min immersion period were then extracted.
Mean values across the 10-min immersion were used for the primary pod comparisons.
For secondary time-course analyses, the immersion period was additionally divided into four successive 2.5-min intervals.
EEG metrics were derived from mean log10-transformed wavelet power (Fig. 3(B) in the main text).

text.text: Frontal alpha (8-12 Hz) and beta (13-30 Hz) power were averaged across F3, Fz, and F4; beta was additionally separated into low-beta (13-19 Hz) and high-beta (20-30 Hz) exploratory measures.
Frontal midline theta (FMT) was calculated as theta-band power (4-7 Hz) at Fz.
The log theta-beta ratio (TBR) was calculated as log10 theta power minus log10 beta power averaged across F3, Fz, and F4.

Frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) was calculated as right-minus-left log10 alpha power for homologous frontal electrode pairs, with F4-F3 designated as the primary FAA measure and F8-F7 and Fp2-Fp1 included as exploratory measures.
Secondary task-to-immersion analyses characterized EEG differences between the preimmersion serial-subtraction period and subsequent seated immersion.
For each EEG outcome, task-period activity was compared with mean activity across the 10-min immersion period using participant-level estimates pooled across pod sessions.

Because participants responded aloud during the serial-subtraction task whereas they observed their surroundings without speaking during immersion, these analyses were interpreted as differences between experimental periods that could reflect cognitive, behavioral, speech-related, and electrophysiological differences, rather than as evidence of physiological stress recovery.
For task-to-immersion comparisons, normality of paired immersion-minus-task difference scores was assessed using Shapiro-Wilk tests.

Paired t tests were used when the Shapiro-Wilk test was nonsignificant (p > .05), whereas Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used when paired difference scores deviated significantly from normality (p ≤ .05).
